title: Put on mercy (Colossians 3:12–17)
hook: put on mercy, kindness, humility, and above all charity

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thank-you note from prison: I have learned to be content. Your line was I have learned. What did you name as already enough? Day five hundred ninety-two.

Some clothes change how you stand. A uniform on the first day of a job. A borrowed suit at a funeral. The jersey of your team on game day. Paul writes to Colossae, a small town in what's now Turkey, to a church he seems never to have visited. And in the third chapter he talks about getting dressed. First, take off the old self like a worn-out coat: anger, malice, lying. Then, he says, here is what to put on.
screen: `CLOTHES THAT CHANGE HOW YOU STAND.` → `A CHURCH PAUL NEVER VISITED.` → `TAKE OFF THE OLD, PUT ON THE NEW.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Put ye on therefore, as the elect of God, holy, and beloved, the bowels of mercy, benignity, humility, modesty, patience." Bowels of mercy sounds strange to us, but it's honest about the body. The Greek word means the inner organs, the gut, where people of that time felt compassion. We'd say heart. A mercy you feel in your stomach. Then the five garments: mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience. Then what they're for: "Bearing with one another, and forgiving one another, if any have a complaint against another: even as the Lord hath forgiven you, so do you also." Paul doesn't pretend there will be no complaints. He assumes there will be, and tells them what to wear when it happens. Then the last piece: "But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection." Bond is the same word we met in Ephesians: syndesmos, the binding. A chapter earlier Paul used it for the bands that hold a body together. Charity is what holds the other virtues together. Without it, they come apart. Then the chapter widens. Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, singing psalms and hymns. And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks. Catholic priests have an old custom that puts this on the body. For centuries, as a priest put on each vestment before Mass, he said a short prayer for a matching virtue: purity with the cincture tied at the waist, for one. The prayers are now optional, but some priests still say them.
screen: `BOWELS OF MERCY: FELT IN THE GUT.` · `FIVE GARMENTS.` · `FOR WHEN THERE'S A COMPLAINT.` · `CHARITY: THE BOND THAT HOLDS IT ALL.` · then, large: `ABOVE ALL THESE THINGS HAVE CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one garment, one person. Settle, and breathe. Paul's list is for the day a complaint comes, so start there. Think of the person most likely to bring you a complaint today, or to get one from you. Of the five, which would you most need with them: mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, or patience? Choose just one. Then touch the last thing you'll put on before you go out, a jacket, a watch, your shoes, and give it that word. If you pray, you can say Paul's line as you touch it: above all these things have charity. If you don't, let the cloth carry the word for you. The bell holds the time.
Syndesmos, the binding. The word Paul uses for charity, which holds together mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Today's word.
Your line: above all, charity. Today, when you meet that person, touch the thing you gave the word to, and wear it. Day five hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Traditionally, a priest says a short vesting prayer as he puts on each vestment before Mass; the prayers are optional today but still used by some, and many Catholics pray a morning offering at the start of the day.

original.note: Greek: the inner organs, the seat of compassion; 'bowels of mercy' (Colossians 3:12).

trapdoor: what it means: dress yourself every day in mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, and tie it all with charity.
what a scholar hears: splanchna, gut-deep compassion; syndesmos again, the binding; the vesting prayers of the old sacristy.

notes: Colossians 2:1 indicates Paul had not visited Colossae; Epaphras as founder (1:7). Pauline authorship of Colossians is debated among scholars; not raised in the voice.

The voice lists the five garments as 'mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience' (modern renderings of the Greek); the DR quote just before says 'benignity ... modesty'. Confirm listeners won't be confused.

Review edit: 'a church he had never visited' softened to 'seems never to have visited' (inferred from 2:1); 'many priests still say them' changed to 'some'; howItsDone no longer claims Catholics pray the morning offering 'as they dress'.
Vesting prayers: in the pre-1970 Missal; optional now. The voice names only the cincture–purity pairing. Confirm.

Audit (second sample): the practice (give a piece of clothing a virtue) and the 'belt' picture for charity repeated day 586's armor-of-God practice (touch helmet, breastplate, belt, shoes, one word each). The practice now starts from the complaint in 3:13 and one garment, and charity is pictured with syndesmos as the bands of a body (Colossians 2:19) instead of a belt.
